02
01 · The problem

The first 1000 days decide 90% of a child's brain development.
India spends them under-supported.

Infant mortality · 202425.8 per 1,000 live births
Brain development90% inside the first 1000 days
Crying, per day2–3 HRS normal for a young infant
What that adds up to, at 3 a.m.
  • Normal crying is the most common trigger for caregiver crisis — and it arrives exactly when the household is most exhausted.
  • Nobody is awake to ask. A quarter of mothers have no one in the house to turn to, and the questions are urgent: is this normal, is this medicine safe while I am feeding her, has she fed enough?

04
02 · The product

It tries to settle her first — then checks whether that worked.

Nothing happens first

A fuss that resolves itself is not an event. The first twelve seconds are logged silently.

Your voice goes first

Recorded lullabies outrank every built-in sound. Volume is capped at 55% — this plays a metre from an infant's ear.

It measures, not assumes

Settled means a settling trend or an 18 dB drop from peak. The answer is recorded either way.

It learns this baby

A smoothed success rate per sound, with 15% exploration so the first thing that worked is not played forever.

The verification step is the product. No monitor on the market attempts to settle the baby, and none of them check.
05
02 · One baby, every screen

The phone watches the cot. The alert finds you wherever you are.

Stepped out to the shop?

The watch buzzes on your wrist with the severity in the pattern, and the alert names what Nila already tried.

Working in the next room?

Open the dashboard on a second phone or the laptop. Live status, the night's timeline, no app to install.

Both parents, one baby

Every paired device receives the same state at the same time. There is no primary account and nothing to log into.

06
02 · What it remembers

One entry per cry, and a week a parent can read.

The monitor is for 3 a.m. The dashboard under it is for ten the next morning — nobody studies a chart while a baby is screaming, and is this getting worse is a question the live screen cannot answer.
Derived from rows you can read yourself
  • Crying against the three-hour line, day by day. The Wessel colic definition is purely a duration — which is why this app may measure it, and why measuring it is not a diagnosis.
  • Sleep as a curve you touch for any day’s exact hours. A day nobody logged is a gap, not a zero: we forgot to tap and she did not sleep are different facts.
  • A donut of what the sound suggested, carrying as its own wedge the share of cries the cause model would not name.
  • Light and dark from every screen’s top bar, and one theme file every palette reads — so a medicine verdict cannot land on a pale card in an app just put into dark mode.
Sleep

A stopwatch, not a log

Tap to start, tap to stop, elapsed time on the button’s face. It used to write a timestamp and no end — a log no duration could be recovered from, and no chart drawn.

Timeline

One cry, one entry

A cry writes six rows: heard, played, judged, woke you, ended. They fold into one entry with the steps a tap underneath, so one bad evening no longer pushes two days off the screen.

Evidence

The cry a doctor can hear

Woke you, ran to the cap, or came back as pain: that one keeps its audio for 30 days and plays from the timeline. A parent walks in with a recording instead of a recollection.

The app already held every row this needed and showed none of it, because a list of events is a record, not an answer.

03 · Phone-first · Built for the Snapdragon NPU

Every inference runs on your iQOO.

Tried in this order, each verified with a real inference
What that buys, overnight
  • A whole night on one battery. Below −55 dBFS the pipeline skips inference entirely, which in a quiet nursery is nearly every window.
  • Never a surprise at 3 a.m. A delegate that builds successfully can still fail on its first real frame, so each one is probed before it is trusted.
  • Provable on stage, and inside the app. One tap runs the real path on the real accelerator; Insights then keeps score live — which delegate took the graph, the detector’s p95 on this handset, and how little of a quiet night gets past the silence gate to reach it.
iQOO 15 · Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 · 80 TOPS Hexagon NPU · arm64-v8a · minSdk 26 · second screen on port 8787 over the LAN · TensorFlow Lite, ONNX Runtime and MediaPipe, all on device

04 · The three intelligence pipelines

Retrieval, medicine safety, and vision — each one staged.

Asking a question · offline RAG
46 sourced documents
Route it firstemergency · dose · diagnosis · distress · too vague · off topic
RetrieveBM25 keyword ranking over 46 docs · title ×4 · keywords ×3
Filterby audience and the baby's age in months
Answerthe retrieved text, verbatim, with its source
Shorten, optionallyQwen 0.5B · checked for overlap, quantities and polarity
Checking a medicine · five agents
98% accuracy · drug–drug interaction
1 · Historyher conditions, mined from her own records
2 · ReadPP-OCRv4 · rotated, upside down, white on foil
3 · Identifyexact tokens, then fuzzy — 1BUPROFENA00 → ibuprofen
4 · Interactagainst her allergies, conditions and current medicines
5 · Adjudicaterules only · the worst finding always wins
Watching the cot · two signals
every frame, all night
Always onBlazeFace presence + frame-difference motion, every frame
Something changedthe face is gone — but which of the several meanings is it?
One frame, one questionPOSITION · FACE · CONCERN · DOING — a closed vocabulary
Parse strictlyanything outside the vocabulary is discarded, not shown
Alert only on concernuncertainty is never an alert · frames never touch disk
One rule holds across all three. A language model never supplies a fact, is never shown a health record, and is nowhere near the medicine verdict — it phrases what retrieval already found, and its output is dropped if it drifts.
Drug–drug interaction accuracy measured on the DrugBank dataset.
13
04 · The model at the centre of it

The fastest and most accurate baby cry model.

Household sounds it does not fire on
vacuum cleanerwashing machine door knockcan opening coughingcat sirencar horn crying baby · 8 of 8
Why it is this good
  • Hard-negative mining. Every training negative was scored with the trained model and the hardest 18% oversampled — cats, laughter, roosters, crows, toilet flush. Cry F1 rose from 0.922 to 0.942 and the household false alarms went to zero.
  • A frontend that is a known quantity. 25 ms frames, 10 ms hop, 64 mel bands from 125 to 7500 Hz — and infant cry fundamentals sit at 300–600 Hz, right in the middle of it.
  • Written twice and pinned together. The transform exists in Python for training and Kotlin for inference; a golden fixture holds them within 0.002, so the phone sees exactly the distribution the model was trained on.
  • Quantised, then re-checked. Compressing to 38 KB moved the AUC by 0.00006 — which is why the small model is the one that ships.
Tested on the Donate-a-Cry corpus · subject-wise held-out infants, no infant in both halves · 2,946 test clips
14
05 · Cost to the family

No second device. No subscription. No cloud bill.

Why an iQOO makes it better
  • The Snapdragon NPU keeps detection instant with the screen off and the phone on charge beside the cot.
  • An infrared emitter. Nila turns the fan or AC down at the first soothing attempt. Very few phones ship one — iQOO does, and Nila speaks NEC frames to it.
The market it opens
  • Asia-Pacific is the fastest-growing baby-monitor market in the world at roughly 10.9% a year, and India is most of that growth.
  • India has 700+ million smartphones and a spare handset in a great many drawers. That is the installed base Nila ships to on day one.
Who it reaches that hardware cannot
  • Homes with no broadband, where a cloud monitor is simply not a product.
  • Families for whom ₹25,000 is not a baby purchase — which is most of them.
15
05 · Privacy

Private by construction, not by policy.

No network requests

Cleartext is forbidden outright in the manifest. The app holds no API keys, because it calls no APIs — there is nothing in the build to extract.

Only the cry, and only if you allow it

The night is analysed in memory and discarded, window by window. Only a declared cry is written — 7 days, or 30 for the ones a doctor might want to hear — into app-private storage no other app can read. One switch turns even that off, and off means the recorder is never opened.

Backup is disabled

Turned off in the manifest, so health documents for the baby and the mother cannot leave by a cloud transport even by accident.

No account, no analytics

Nothing to sign up for and nothing measured about you. The second screen is off until you switch it on, and refuses anything but a local address.

Seven guardrails, all of them local
Emergency20+ phrasings — not breathing, blue lips, seizure, choking
Dose requestsAlways refused. The build fails if a dose appears in the corpus
DiagnosisDeclines, and says what to observe and when to seek care
Caregiver distressSafe immediate action first, then helpline numbers
Age gatingNewborn guidance never returns for a nine-month-old
Audience routingHer questions reach the 27 documents written for her
Relevance floorSays it has nothing rather than offering the nearest paragraph
A demo that works anywhere
  • It seeds itself with an example family — a four-month-old, her mother's record with a penicillin allergy, a day of feeds and a week of crying — so no screen is ever empty on a device nobody has used.
  • No time in it is a date. Recent events are offsets from install — "95 minutes ago" — and the daily routine carries a clock time on a past day, so the charts’ hour axis and the family’s nights agree. A build made today still describes this week when it is installed next month.
  • It runs on a plane, in a browser and in a hall with no signal, which is exactly where this is being judged.
Nila is an awareness aid. It reports what a microphone and a camera can establish — crying, its duration, its direction, whether a face is visible and whether there is movement. Knowing precisely where that line sits is what makes everything on the right side of it trustworthy.
16
05 · Impact and what comes next

A monitor that settles the baby, on a phone already in the house.

What changes
  • The household stops being woken unnecessarily. Two rungs run before any alert, so a baby who would have self-settled does — and the parent who is woken is woken for a reason, with that reason attached.
  • The alert follows the parent. Wrist, second phone or laptop, with the severity readable by feel — so nobody has to sit in the room to be on duty.
  • The mother is a user, not a bystander. 27 of the 46 entries are hers: diet, lactation, recovery, mental health, and twenty medicine monographs checked against her own allergies and conditions.
  • The appointment stops being a guess. A week of crying against the three-hour line, the hours it clusters in, and the audio of the cries that woke somebody — a parent walks in with a measurement and a recording instead of a recollection of a bad fortnight.
  • It works where the network does not — a village, a train, a basement ward, a power cut. The app cannot tell the difference, because it never asks.
What comes next
  • On-device personalisation. A few minutes of one specific baby's cry, fine-tuning the final layer on the handset itself — learning that never leaves the phone, which is the natural next step for a device this capable.
  • Ten Indian languages. The language field already runs through the profile, router and retriever; the corpus is next, with human review.
  • A 200-entry knowledge base, widening from crying and medicines into night weaning, reflux, stool changes and growth.
  • A shared night. Two caregivers, one baby, alternating who is on call — the device mesh already carries everything that needs.
